tagline: Along the Klamath and Trinity, a river road with a Bigfoot namesake
intro: Highway 96 follows the Klamath and Trinity rivers through Northern California. The Forest Service lists Bigfoot among three scenic byways through Klamath National Forest, describing its stretch along the Klamath from Happy Camp to Orleans. The highway account identifies the longer Happy Camp–Willow Creek corridor as a National Forest Scenic Byway. Along the lower Trinity, Hoopa Valley opens above Campbell Creek and narrows again at Bald Hill. The route passes through Six Rivers National Forest between Orleans and Weitchpec, where Highway 169 branches away from Highway 96.

The Forest Service gave this stretch of Highway 96 its Bigfoot name. Happy Camp gives the name a physical form with an 18-foot statue made from recycled metal. The road also links much older places: Orleans occupies the Karuk settlement of Panamnik, and Weitchpec is an ancestral Yurok village predating European contact. Gold-rush miners named Happy Camp during their early prosperity. The Karuk Tribe is headquartered there now, giving the town a present role beyond its mining-era name.

From Happy Camp, follow the Klamath toward Orleans and then Weitchpec. At the confluence, Highway 96 leaves the Klamath and follows the Trinity upstream through Hoopa to Willow Creek, where it meets Highway 299.

moments.title: Happy Camp
moments.text: An 18-foot Bigfoot made of recycled metal gives Happy Camp a visible link to the byway’s name. The Happy Camp Community Council also hosts the annual Bigfoot Jamboree. Gold-rush miners gave the town its English name during their early prosperity. Its Karuk name is athithúf-vuunupma, and the Karuk Tribe has its headquarters here. The town sits on the Klamath River where a network of creeks includes Elk Creek and Indian Creek. Happy Camp is also an administrative base for the Forest Service’s Happy Camp/Oak Knoll Ranger Districts in Klamath National Forest.
moments.notice: Happy Camp’s Bigfoot statue is 18 feet tall and made of recycled metal.

moments.title: Orleans
moments.text: Panamnik is the Karuk name for Orleans and the name of the original Indigenous settlement here. European-American miners called their settlement New Orleans Bar. In 1855 it became Orleans Bar and the seat of Klamath County, a county that no longer exists. Orleans lies within the historical territory of the Karuk Tribe of California. It is also within Six Rivers National Forest, with a district ranger’s office, on Highway 96 northeast of Weitchpec. The community is the nearest inhabited place to the remote site of the Patterson–Gimlin film of a purported Bigfoot, about ten miles northeast.

moments.title: Weitchpec
moments.text: The Trinity joins the Klamath at Weitchpec, where Highways 96 and 169 also meet. This ancestral Yurok village was known as Weitspus and was a major Yurok settlement before European contact. One temporary nineteenth-century name, Durkee’s Ferry, recalled the ferry Clark W. Durkee operated here in 1851. Weitchpec is within the Yurok reservation and has a Yurok Tribal Office and Community Center. The village lay in Klamath County from 1851, then became part of Humboldt County after 1874. For the southbound drive, the confluence marks the change from following the Klamath to following the Trinity toward Hoopa.
